title: How Internships Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss internships: their history from medical apprenticeships and co-ops (Northeastern University, 1909) to today's widespread programs; survey statistics on job offers from internships (NACE 2013 and 2016) and average paid intern wages; the Fair Labor Standards Act six-point test for unpaid internships at for-profit companies; the 2011 Fox Searchlight (Black Swan) lawsuit by interns Eric Glatt and Alex Footman and the judge's revised test; other intern lawsuits (Condé Nast, Viacom, MGM); ethics of unpaid internships, exploitation, and nepotism/cronyism; and tips for finding internships. Includes a Secret Service listener mail segment at the end.

entities.name: National Association of Colleges and Employers

segments.title: Opening banter and internship experiences
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about interns being mistreated, their own lack of internships in college, and a statistic on college graduates doing internships rising from the 1980s to the mid-2000s. They note the term data is plural and mention the film about interns shot in Atlanta.

segments.title: Internship job offer statistics and unpaid internship trends
segments.summary: They cite NACE surveys showing over 70 percent of paid internships led to job offers, up from about 60 percent in 2013, versus about 37 percent for unpaid internships and 36.5 percent for those with no internship. They discuss millennials taking multiple unpaid internships, the gig economy, and how reliance on parents excludes less wealthy people.

segments.title: Nepotism, cronyism and inequality in internships
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how internships often come through connections, which favors wealthier families, and reference the book Dream Hoarders on how advantage is perpetuated. They label this cronyism and nepotism.

segments.title: History of the intern and co-op programs
segments.summary: The term intern comes from medicine, where after World War I doctors-in-training worked in hospitals. Companies later formalized internships with universities, and the earliest one cited was at Northeastern University around 1909, called a co-op. Use grew in the 1960s and between 1970 and 1983 university co-op or internship offerings rose from 200 to 1,000. The hosts distinguish co-ops from internships.

segments.title: Are internships necessary and which fields benefit
segments.summary: Josh argues internships are useful in STEM, psychology, political science, and economics, where field-specific jargon, software, and connections are learned. Media and entertainment companies are described as the most likely places for exploitation, with anecdotes about being asked to do personal errands.

segments.title: Fair Labor Standards Act criteria for unpaid internships
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the six Department of Labor criteria for legally unpaid internships at private for-profit businesses, including training similar to an educational environment, benefit to the intern, no displacement of regular employees, close supervision, no immediate advantage to the employer, no job entitlement, and no expectation of wages. Nonprofit interns are considered volunteers.

segments.title: 2011 Fox Searchlight Black Swan lawsuit and other intern settlements
segments.summary: Interns Eric Glatt and Alex Footman sued Fox Searchlight Pictures in 2011 over unpaid work on Black Swan and won; a judge in 2013 in the Second Circuit set a different test, and Fox settled in 2016. The hosts also cover the 2014 Condé Nast class action settlement of $5.8 million, Viacom's roughly $7.2 million settlement in 2013, and an MGM settlement. Companies changed internship programs in response.

segments.title: Finding internships and making yourself valuable
segments.summary: Hosts advise making yourself invaluable during an internship and suggest resources such as LinkedIn, InternTips, Media Bistro, ZipRecruiter, and intern blogs. They encourage speaking up about exploitation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Secret Service presidential protection
segments.summary: A listener shares an anonymous story from a former colleague of a Secret Service presidential protective detail member, describing a credible threat in which agents took charge of the president and rerouted his motorcade against his will, and explaining why experience matters for the job.
